full_judgment:
2. The appellant as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for eviction of the defendant Nos. 1-5 .from the suit premises and for realisation of arrear rents and compensation for unauthoriscd occupation of the suit premises. The case of the plaintiff in short, was that the premises in suit belonged to him and one Abul Meah, predecessor of the defendants Nos. 1 to 4, was a monthly tenant under him at a rental of Tk. 8/- per month. Abul Miah defaulted in payment of the rent. On his death his heirs, the defendant Nos. 1-4, continued in possession of the suit premises but they also not only defaulted in payment of rents from the month of February, 1971 in spite of the demands made by the plaintiff to pay the rents but also sub-let the premises to defendant No.5. The plaintiffs further case was that he required the premises bonafide for his own use and occupation and he terminated the tenancy with the expiry of the last day of February, 1971 by serving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act through registered post. He claimed compensation at the rate of Tk. 21-per diem for unauthorised occupation since the termination of the tenancy. 

 3. Defendants No. 1, 4 and 5 contested the suit by filing written statement. Their case was that they had been possessing the suit premises on payment of rents and they were not defaulters and there was no arrear of rent from February, 1971 as alleged since they deposited the rent duly in the Office of the Controller in House Rent Control Case No. 70 of 1971 and the allegation of sub-letting was false as defendant No.5 was their partner in the business. The notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was neither tendered nor they refused to accept the same and as such there was no service of notice determining the tenancy. The plea of bona fide requirement of the premises was false as the plaintiff had many other residential houses in the town. 

 4. The learned Munsif decreed the suit in part holding that the defendants were defaulters and the plaintiff was entitled to get Tk. 192/- as arrears of rent. Against that decree the defendants preferred the aforesaid appeal and the plaintiff also filed cross-appeal. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal on contest and dismissed the cross-appeal. 

 5. Mr. Nirmalendu Bikahs Dutta contends that the Court of appeal below erred in law in holding that there was no cause of action for the suit and the defendants were not defaulters as they were depositing the rents in the office of House Rent Controller on an erroneous view of the provision of President's Order No. 12 of 1972. He further submits that admittedly the rents for the months of March to June, 1971 having had been deposited in the office of the House Rent Controller in lump on 17.6.71 the ten- ants were not protected under section 18 (1) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. Thirdly, the lower appellate Court erred in holding that the plaintiff did not require the premises for bona fide use and occupation as he had some other houses. 

 6. The Court of appeal held that by reason of the provision of President's Order No. 12 of 1972 the respondents were not defaulters as they were de- positing the rents in the Office of the Controller although the deposits were made not in accordance with the provision of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. Article 4 of the Presider it’s Order No. 12 or 1972 reads as:- Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for time being in force, in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any legal proceeding by or under any law, the period between the 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972 (both days inclusive), shall be excluded." 

 7. Provisions of section 4 has no manner of application to a case where the tenants deposit the arrear rents in the Office of the Controller at a time in lump for several months since section 4, it seem to me, only excludes the period between 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972 in computing the period of limitation for instituting any legal proceeding by or under any law. I am of the opinion that Section 4 contemplates a legal proceeding which could not be instituted within the prescribed period of limitation due to reign of terror perpetrated by Pakistan occupation army and became time-barred. In the instant case the defendants having had already deposited the rents in the Office of the Controller the question of exclusion of the period as contained in section 4 of the Order docs not arise and the defendants cannot take the plea that since they had been depositing the rent in the Office of the Controller they are not defaulters. Provision of Section 4 of the Order docs not save default. It saves a legal proceeding from being barred under the relevant law by extending the period of limitation adding to it the period from 1st March, 1971 to 1st March, 1972. Even assuming that they are within time to deposit the rent in the Office of the Rent Controller in view of the provision of section 4 of the Order still in my opinion they are not protected since a lump deposit of rent for several months at a time is contrary to the provision of section 19 (I) of the Premises Rent control Ordinance, 1963 and section 4 of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972 docs not lend any support to the tenants. It is evident from the judgment of the lower appellate Court that on several occasions the defendants deposited the rents of several months at different times in lump as was found by it on the basis of Ext. A series, the challahs showing deposits of rents. The lower appellate Court found that the defendants deposited the rents for 4moTItfrS from March to June, 1971 on 17.6.1971 at a time in lump. The deposit of rent in the Office of the Controller protects a tenant only where the deposit is made on the refusal of the landlord to accept the rent remitted by postal money order within a fortnight of the date on which rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered. In the instant case there is nothing on the record to show that the defendants remitted the arrear rent within the time prescribed in Section 18(5) of the Ordinance. On the other hand, as earlier indicated the rents for the months of March, 1971 to June 1971 was deposited on 17.6.71. Therefore it is evident that arrears rents were remitted long after the period prescribed for remitting the rent by postal money order as the rent for the month of March, 197i was to be remitted fly postal money order by the fifteenth day 9t April1971 and in view of Explanation.to' Sub-section (5) of Section 18, the landlord sh.pl not be deemed to have refused to accept the tent. Remittance of-rein by   postal money order to the landlord cannot be equated in meaning with the institution of alleging. Viewed from this angle it can easily be concluded that such remittance not being a legal proceeding within the meaning of Section 4 of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972 the provisions of Section 4 of the Order has no manner of application to the facts of the instant case. Where the rent remitted by postal money order within the period prescribed in Section 18 (5) of the Ordinance is returned on refusal by the landlord to accept to the tenant as undelivered by the postal authorities the question of deposit by 1st March, 1972 may be considered as deposit in time by reason of Section 4 of the Order. But such consideration will lead to another question'. It is whether deposit of rent in the Office of the Controller is a legal, proceeding. According to Section 2 of the Order legal proceeding includes suit, case, prosecution, appeal, revision and review. Deposit of rent in the Office of the Controller is not a suit, a prosecution, an appeal, a revision and a review. The question is it a case within the meaning of section 2 of the Order? The Rent Controller receives rent like any other counter and he does not determine whether the allegations made in the application for deposit arc true or false. The object in accepting such rent is to furnish evidence of tender as kept by the office of the Controller in order to decide the question of default in a properly constituted suit. In this view of the matter, the deposit of rent in the Office of the Controller is not an institution of a 'case' as the Controller upon sue deposit docs not decide the dispute between the tenant and the landlord. In such a situation the Controller ill a mere 'conduit pipe'. Viewed from this angle also I am of the Opinion that deposit of rent in the Office of the Controller by filing an application is not a 'case' within the meaning of section 2 of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972 and section 4 of the Order has no role to play in this case. In this respect the decision reported in 8 D.L.R. 272 may profitably be referred to. Moreover, the intention of the law makers to promulgate the Order was to enable persons to institute any legal proceeding which could not be instituted due to atrocities perpetrated by Pakistan occupation army disrupting the normal life and activities. The tenants in this case already having had submitted to the jurisdiction of the Controller cannot take the advantage of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972. 

 9. In this case as it is found that the notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act was duly served, the plaintiff is entitled to a decree for eviction, arrear rents and compensation. The argument on cross-appeal has no substance as I 'do not find that the Courts below erred in allowing part decree for area, rents.
